The nomadic hunter-gatherers who had laboriously earned their place on Earth organized into small groups, differentiating social roles, building the first settlements, and initiating a great revolution. Scientists call this period "Mesolithic", and this game talks about those people. In MESOS, you are the leader of an ancient tribe, and as such, your role is to nurture the growth of your tribe by adding new members, ensuring its sustenance, constructing buildings, and addressing unfolding events. Each round, you must place your totem pawn on the offer track, then following the pawns' order on the track, you will acquire character or building cards and add them to your tribe. Each card has specific effects and may earn prestige points (PP) as you construct specialized buildings and prepare wisely for the events you will face. Whoever manages to bring the most prestige to their tribe wins. Number of players: 2 - 5 Game duration: 17 mn Complexity: 2 / 5 Play Mesos and 1414 other games online. Restore the top row 4 Events 5 End of Game 6 Expert Variant 7 Rebalanced Shamans Game Overview In MESOS, you are the leader of an ancient tribe, and as such, your role is to nurture the growth of your tribe by adding new members, ensuring its sustenance, constructing buildings, and addressing unfolding events. Each round, you must place your totem pawn on the offer track, then following the pawns' order on the track, you will acquire character or building cards and add them to your tribe. Each card has specific effects and may earn prestige points (PP) as you construct specialized buildings and prepare wisely for the events you will face. Whoever manages to bring the most prestige to their tribe wins. How to Play A game of MESOS unfolds over 10 rounds until the Tribe cards deck is depleted. In each round, you need to carry out the following two phases, in order: Place Totem pawns on the Offer track Following the order of the Totem pawns on the Turn Order tile, from top to bottom, place your Totem on an available Offer tile (i.e., a tile where there is no other Totem already). Each Offer tile shows a space where you can place your Totem, and the action you must perform (usually the number of cards you can take and the row from where you can take them). Resolve Actions In turn, starting from the player with the leftmost Totem pawn on the Offer track and proceeding to the right, resolve the action indicated on the Offer tile where you placed your Totem. With the exception of tile A (available only in 5-player games), which provides 3 Food tokens, all other Offer tiles allow you to choose and take Character and/or Building cards from the upper and/or lower row, as indicated on the tile itself. You can never take Event cards from any row. If an Offer tile allows you to take multiple cards (even from different rows), you can freely choose the order in which to take them. If, on your turn, there are no more available cards in the rows from which you should take them, you receive nothing. If there are still Character cards available, you must take them. After resolving the action on the Offer tile, return your Totem pawn to the Turn Order tile, placing it in the first available space starting from the top. If the space where you placed your Totem provides a Food bonus, immediately take the specified number of Food tokens. The player placing in the last space must pay 1 Food token if they have one. Only if they don’t have Food to pay, they lose 2 Prestige Points. The arrangement of Totem pawns on the Turn Order tile determines the turn order for the next round. [Rating: 2/10] Online auf BGA gespielt. Haushoch verloren. Wenn man oft das hintere Token hat, kann man ja auch nix mehr wirklich nehmen an Karten. Komischer Mechanismus. Nicht meins.

[Rating: 3/10] Boring set collecion game. Totally unplayable at 2 players. The action selection is unintuitive, barely any difference between cards, and all card types have the same art??? Shocking they still make games like that in 2024. Nothing innovative. The art style is pretty though

[Rating: 3/10] I won this from the BGG Giveaway contest. The art on the cards is just awful and a huge turnoff so I sold this game without playing.

[Rating: 4/10] This is your typical 4 star game, its not so good, but definitely playable in certain scenarios. I love Nidavellir, and this game has glimpses of that, though it’s much simpler and more streamlined. If we stick with the comparison, it’s like one tavern in Nidavellir, where you decide who goes first and who goes last—toward the end players get more cards. The card selection works on a sort of two-tier system, with fresh cards always appearing on top, making them more valuable. You play 10 rounds, and by the end, you’ll typically collect between 20 to 30 cards. The system is very sleek, but it f

[Rating: 4/10] The turn order mechanism is one of my favorite iterations on Kingdomino's -- where you can take the weaker option now for better options later -- that I've seen. But then the rest felt much too much like 7 Wonders, with an added helping of dirty dishes (it seemed like some suits were winners if anybody got to dominate them... so who's going to stop them, you or me?)  [1 play]

[Rating: 4/10] FIRST IMPRESSION:  Meh, it is fine but I don't know that it does anything new. One is basically drafting/purchasing cards for sets for different purposes whether it be end game scoring or in-game scoring events, and turn order is determined by placement. I don't anticipate playing again, but if others want to play I suppose I'd do so - it plays fast.

[Rating: 4/10] Initial Impressions: I think I have to just admit that Luciani when he does small card games is a totally different designer than the mid- to medium-heavy-weight Euros that he excels at. This game felt like any other rote set collection game, the twist here of course the two offers to draft from and turn order. But nothing is particularly interesting. It feels just like Kingdomino, a game I already don't rate that highly, but trading the spatial element for more set collection types.

[Rating: 4/10] It's alright, like many others in the same genre. I guess it would become quickly repetitive?

[Rating: 4.5/10] Gra ma banalne zasady i minimum głębi. Zbieramy karty. Każdy kolor charakteryzuje się w czymś innym. W każdej erze wychodzą wydarzenie, które mogą zapewnić punkty, a także mogą wymusić na nas wykarmienie członków plemienia, czyli zebranych kart. Proste zarządzenie zasobami i tworzenie najlepszych kombinacji z kart. To wszystko. Gra nadaje się ewentualnie dla graczy, którzy bardzo mało grają. W innym przypadku jest masa ciekawszych gier i nie warto na Mesos tracić czasu.  Ocena po 1 partii w 4 osoby. Czas około 30 minut.
